newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU to aid flood victims as German dike bulges.
newsitem.headline: EU to aid flood victims as German dike bulges.

text.p: The European Commission on Friday pledged fast aid for flood victims in Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic as German dikes on the River Oder edged ever nearer to bursting point.

The looming failure of the most fragile dike, at Hohenwutzen, threatened to flood an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's border with Poland, submerging dozens of villages, farms and factories.
"The chances that the dike will break are more probable than that we will be able to hold it," said a spokesman for the flood crisis committee in nearby Bad Freienwalde.

European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies, in charge of regional aid programmes, said the EU could provide around 87 million marks in immediate relief for flood victims and was also considering a broader reconstruction effort.

"We want to see what we can do to stabilise the dikes and build them back up again when the water has gone and afterward get the infrastructure back up and running," she said. "The EU would support a common programme for the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany."

Some of the worst floods in more than a century have devestated Polish and Czech provinces over the past month. For more than a week, soldiers, aid workers and local villagers in eastern Germany have been fighting to keep the water out.
Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from the three-country region in central Europe, where floods have claimed over 100 lives and destroyed homes, farms and livestock.

While there have been no flood-related deaths in Germany, damage to houses and farms has been extensive. Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice as the likelihood of a dam break grows daily.

"I hope it holds for the next seven days," said Manfred Stolpe, premier of Germany's affected Brandenburg state, casting a nervous glance towards soldiers frantically loading sandbags to prop up the dike in Hohenwutzen, on a bend in the Oder.
Cracks also appeared in a 1,200-metre (one mile) stretch of the dam upstream near Reitwein -- the site of a dam break that let in the region's last flood, in 1947.
Brandenburg state officials said the situation in Reitwein was still under control but could become as critical as in Hohenwutzen unless water levels soon fell by at least 1.5 metres (five feet).
Many increasingly despondent German local officials were saying only a miracle could save the Oderbruch river plain with its 800 square km of low-lying fertile farmland.

The Polish government estimates damage from the floods could be as high as $1.4 billion, and German officials have put the cost to their country at around one billion marks ($540 million). In the Czech Republic, economists have said damage could be as high as $2.6 billion.
The floods have torn up roads and highways, contaminated water supply and power, railway and telecommunications networks. Damage to local farms has been extensive.

Oskar Lafontaine, chairman of the opposition Social Democrats, said during a visit that his party would put a motion to the Bonn parliament to request an additional 100 million marks in aid for victims. The government has already earmarked some 200 million marks to compensate families and businesses.
